prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, opening a new regime of precision in the measurement of time
for the discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos with the IceCube detector, opening a new window on the cosmos

statement.case_for: I keep my opening number one, the IceCube neutrino discovery, and pair it with the optical lattice clock because they are the two candidates where a new instrument, not a new idea alone, made the discovery possible, and both have been independently confirmed. Optical lattice clocks (Katori, Ye) have been reproduced in several national and university laboratories and agree at the 1e-18 level; the physics will last because the second is likely to be redefined on this basis and the clocks already test constants and relativistic redshift over millimetres. IceCube opened a genuinely new observational window: a diffuse astrophysical neutrino flux confirmed by independent event classes, then the TXS 0506+056 alert follow-up and the Galactic-plane map. The two parts are distinct achievements, from different subfields, and give a three-person prize (Katori, Ye, Halzen) without anyone having to be cut from within a part. B001 has the strongest first-place support in the opening round (three members) and B021 is the first choice of two, so this pairing also draws on the more committed opening votes rather than on the broadest but more diffuse support.
statement.case_against: The IceCube half is the weakest link in attribution. A single name for a collaboration of hundreds, with AMANDA and DUMAND predecessors and later spokespersons and directors outside the credited list, is exactly the kind of credit I would have to defend in public, and the source-class picture is not settled (TXS and the Galactic plane rest on few objects). The clock half sits close to the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and Jun Ye's comb work already received recognition through that route. Pairing two unrelated topics also looks like a compromise prize, and B024 has far broader support across the committee (seven of eight rank it, five in the top three). If condensed-matter colleagues convince me that B024 can be given a fair three-name allocation, the case for a single topological insulator prize is stronger than for this pairing.

responses.point: Ranks optical lattice clocks first: magic-wavelength lattices with thousands of atoms reach near 1e-18, enable geodesy and constants tests, and the Katori-Ye pair is clean; he flags overlap with the comb (2005) and ion-clock (2012) prizes.
responses.response: I agree on the physics and on the attribution, and I put B001 in my own top three. Where I differ slightly is the overlap worry: the comb and single-ion prizes did not give the many-atom lattice with systematic uncertainty beaten down by magic-wavelength engineering, and independent laboratories now compare clocks at the 1e-18 level, which is the confirmation I look for. I would ask you for one thing. If we pair B001 with something else, does the redefinition of the second being still pending trouble you, or is the demonstrated performance enough?

responses.point: Shares my first place for IceCube, citing the diffuse flux as the firmest part, confirmation by independent analyses and the 2018 coincidence, but questions whether a single Halzen credit is defensible given AMANDA, DUMAND and the collaboration.
responses.response: We agree on the science, and I take his caution on credit seriously; it is my own main reservation. I would not drop the single-name configuration for convenience, but I would like him to say what he would do instead. Naming the diffuse-flux discovery rather than individual sources keeps the citation on the firmest result, and the Statutes limit a prize to three people, so the choice is between one name that follows the concept and construction of IceCube or no IceCube prize at all. I am not yet certain this is right, and that is why IceCube is paired and not proposed alone.

responses.point: Ranks topological insulators first as a general organising principle (bulk invariant and protected boundary states), long confirmed and arguably overdue, with Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan as the trio but a real allocation problem over Mele, Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and Zhang.
responses.response: I accept that B024 is the most broadly supported topic and that its confirmation is the strongest of any candidate; I ranked it fourth only because it lies outside my expertise. My reservation is attribution, not merit. His own ballot says dropping Mele or choosing between Molenkamp and Hasan is a real allocation problem, and the seven members who ranked B024 proposed three different trios. If the condensed-matter members converge on one trio, I would shift to B024 as the main prize, and I name it as my first alternative.

responses.point: Ranks twisted bilayer graphene first: experiment surprising theory, quantitative continuum theory checkable against spectroscopy, many groups reproducing correlated states, with the superconducting pairing still debated.
responses.response: I see the force of the scientific case and the speed with which independent groups reproduced the correlated phases, and I understand why he calls it timely. But the pairing mechanism is open and the discovery is eight years old, so I would rather wait than commit now; my ranking of seventh reflects that. We also differ on names: his trio takes Andrei and leaves out Bistritzer, mine does the reverse, and a credit that two members cannot agree on among themselves is a warning sign, not a detail.

responses.point: Ranks circuit QED first as a clean, fully controllable basic-physics demonstration that became the dominant superconducting-qubit architecture, and notes the 2025 adjacency.
responses.response: I think his own ballot answers the main worry: he lists the 2025 adjacency and the omission of Girvin and Devoret as unresolved, and lindroth-eva and kroll-stefan ranked it eighth and seventh, citing that same overlap. I find the 2025 prize and this one hard to separate in the public mind, and credit within Yale and ETH is intertwined with people not on the list. I do not rule it out, but it has not persuaded me to move B029 into my configuration, and I welcome his own note that he may be biased by his field.

uncertainties: Whether a single-name IceCube credit (Halzen) can be defended against collaboration-scale and AMANDA/DUMAND arguments, or whether the committee prefers to avoid IceCube this year.
Whether the committee would accept two unrelated achievements sharing the prize when B024 and B013 have far wider support among the members.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second, and overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes, change the weight of the clock work.
I am outside condensed matter and atomic physics and cannot independently resolve the B024 and B013 credit questions, which decide whether either becomes the main prize.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for Katori, Ye or Halzen. I work in the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaborations and in the same astroparticle community as IceCube, so I have field familiarity with the IceCube candidate, but no stated collaboration, institutional or personal link to the credited names.
